messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Bank Teller
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Known People: Related people, Stress: Stress, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt, Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
  Negative Appraisals: Inadequacy: I am inadequate, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Robert Miller was sixty-two years old, a bank teller for nearly thirty years, when he became the cause of another person’s devastation. It happened on a Tuesday evening, eight months ago, as he drove home from work. He had felt the usual pressure of the day—a long queue, a fussy customer demanding change, the slow tick of the clock—and he was tired, more tired than he wanted to admit. The light at the intersection of Oak and Fourth turned yellow just as he approached. He thought he could make it. He accelerated. What he did not see was the man stepping off the curb—a man in a dark coat, with a dog by his side. The impact was a sickening thud, a sound Robert still hears in fragments, suddenly, without warning. The man, later identified as Arthur, a father of two, suffered a severe traumatic brain injury. He survived but would never walk or speak the same way again. Robert was not charged. The police report called it an accident. But Robert knew—he had been the one at the wheel.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not fade. It came back whole, with the same raw terror he had felt in that frozen second after the crash—the open mouth, the silence, the blood. And with it came guilt so heavy it felt like a weight in his chest, a guilt that told him he had done something unforgivable. He began to see Arthur’s wife in the bank, a quiet woman who came in every other Friday to deposit a check. She never looked at him directly, but her presence alone was enough to make his hands shake. He started to avoid the teller window on Fridays, swapping shifts with a younger colleague, but he could not avoid her entirely. Sometimes she appeared at the next window, and he would feel his throat tighten. Anything stressful—a long line, a computer glitch, a sudden demand from a customer—set him on edge in the same way, because stress reminded him of that Tuesday evening, of his own fatigue and poor judgment.

His body remained on guard. At night, when his wife, Ellen, turned off the light and settled beside him, Robert lay still, listening. He could not let himself drift off because he needed to stay alert—for what, he was not sure, but he was certain something bad would happen if he let his guard down. Even at home, in the living room he had painted himself, he could not relax. He would sit in his recliner with his hands clasped, watching the door, scanning for clues of danger. At work, he was hypervigilant, watching every customer’s hand, every unexpected movement. A colleague who tapped his shoulder to ask a question made him flinch so violently that he dropped a stack of deposit slips. He had come to believe that his reactions since the accident proved he was a lousy coper, a man who could not handle what life threw at him. He felt inadequate, fundamentally broken, permanently changed for the worse. The old Robert—the one who joked with customers and slept through the night—was gone.

Avoidance crept into every part of his life. He stopped driving altogether, taking the bus to work along a route that avoided Oak and Fourth. He stopped going to the grocery store on weekends because the crowds and the unpredictable contact with strangers felt unbearable. He told Ellen he was just tired, but she had noticed how he withdrew—how he sat through dinner without speaking, how he flinched when she touched his arm to get his attention. Their marriage grew quiet, a silence filled with unspoken worry. At work, his manager pulled him aside twice about his difficulty concentrating and his jumpiness with customers. Robert feared he was one mistake away from being let go.

What finally brought him to seek help was a morning he could not get out of bed. He lay there, staring at the ceiling, unable to muster the strength to face another day of scanning faces and waiting for the next intrusive piece of memory to break through. Ellen found him there, still dressed in his work clothes from the night before. She insisted he call a therapist. Now, sitting in the waiting room, Robert is afraid—afraid that talking about it will make the fragments more vivid, afraid that he will never feel like himself again, but also quietly hoping that someone might tell him this is not proof of how broken he is.
